utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness which, as I understand, will be Karolj Dondo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Dondo, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, Mr. Dondo, before you give testimony. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dondo. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you'll first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, can you confirm to the Court one matter, first of all, that you can speak the English language.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you have chosen to give your evidence today in court in your own language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you have brought into court with you copies of your statements that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor as well as the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Both, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you need to refer to those documents as hard copies at any stage, please inform us and the Court that that is what you want to do. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dondo. First of all, I would like you to see a copy of the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution in the year 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Might the first page of that statement be put on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll see it on the right-hand side screen, Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, this is a copy of your statement that you gave to the Defence, but we will start with that. For some reason it was on my list at the top. If you could just look at that statement there, can you see your signature on the bottom of the statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I can see my initials, yes, the ones that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this is a statement that you gave to the Defence and that you have read this statement and affirmed its content?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just look at the last page of the statement, you're looking at it in the hard copy. Just look at it on the screen, Mr. Dondo. Can you see your statement signed at the end by you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that that statement contained certain corrections that you made in relation to a statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2005?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, some minor corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we now turn to that statement which is 65 ter 2D00-729, and if we could turn to the front page of that statement. If we could move to the signatures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, do you confirm there the front page of a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 9th of March, 2005?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do confirm that this is my signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can we turn to the last page of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you confirm your signature at the end of that statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't be looking at all the pages in between, with Your Honour's leave. Everybody knows they have been signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, is the statements that you have given, first of all to the Office of the Prosecution and then to the Defence with the corrections that you made to your statement to the Prosecutor, taking that into account, is the information contained within those two statements to the best of your knowledge and belief true and correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you today the same questions that made up the information within those two statements, would your answers today be the same answers as you have given on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: They would unless I forgot to mention something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances might the -- first of all, the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, 2D00-729, with made an exhibit in the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number for the 2005 statement would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D1695 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, might the statement given to the Defence, 2D00-730 be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the 2009 statement to the Defence would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, for a point of reference, there is at paragraph 3, line 31 of the statement taken by the Defence, Exhibit D1696, the Court will see there reference to a document seen earlier in evidence last week with a witness, Mr. Lukovic. It has the reference OBR06-23. That has already been admitted into evidence as D1689, which I hope assists the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, could we now look at another document, 2D00-731.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is mentioned in the Defence statement at -- in the English page 7, paragraph 17, line 20, it's in the body of Mr. Dondo's statement. Might I have permission to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, might I now make this document an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, no objections --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- against 2D00-731 to be admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1697 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is 2D00-732. This is mentioned in the Defence statement, Your Honour, at page 9, paragraph 21, line 8. It's a document referred to as OBR05-168. I request leave to add it to our 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to have it admitted, may I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 2D00-732 would receive number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1698.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1698 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is 2D00-692. Your Honour, this is within the Defence statement at page 7, paragraph 17, line 28, where it has the reference OBR05-165. This is already on the 65 ter exhibit list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any objection against admission? Mr. Registrar, 2D00-692 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1699.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1699 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is 2D00-733, referred to at page 11 of the Defence statement, paragraph 27, line 19, may this document be added to the 65 ter exhibit list, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And once leave is granted, I take it to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then 2D00-733, Mr. Registrar, would receive ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1700 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document -- the next document, Your Honour, is 65 ter 2670. It's a document referred to in the Defence statement, page 15, paragraph 38, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in the confidential appendix the number appears a bit odd, it's 26 (0), but that's now, as you said, 2670. That is clear. Any objections, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 2670 would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1701.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1701 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the last of these documents is 65 ter 2676, please. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- referred to in the Defence statement at page 15, paragraph 38, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 2676 would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1702.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1702 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I won't be making a brief summary as to the witness's -- nature of the witness's evidence. I believe this will come out during cross-examination, with the Court's leave, unless the Court wanted me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I do not know what will be -- what will come up during cross-examination, but what Mr. Dondo describes in his statements may be his involvement as a member of the organ that used to liaise, communicate, between the Croatian authorities and the international organisations, and he describes what happened in the early days of August when he was sent to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least the subject matter of the testimony in rather general terms is now available to the public and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I'll just add in one minute as the liaison officer for Sector South he worked under Mr. Lukovic, who gave evidence last week, and he was part of the team of the Croatian military UN/EU liaison group who worked in Knin. He worked with General Cermak. He describes the nature of coordination, meetings that were held at the garrison headquarters. He describes the relationship between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Pasic and other people who were working within Knin at this time, as he describes seeking to normalise life and to get Knin back to a normal state. And he describes the issue of crimes that were being committed at the time and describes Mr. Cermak as passing information on to both the civil and military police from the information passed on to him by the United Nations and other international groups. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before I sit down, Mr. Dondo, I'd like you to look at two documents, or three documents in two sections. The first is 65 ter Exhibit 2D00-755. It's a document dated the 20th of August, 1995. It's not referred to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll seek various leaves after we finish the questioning on the document with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and in order to avoid confusion, you were talking about exhibit numbers, of course they receive the exhibit numbers from the Registry --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whereas, this is the numbering as assigned by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document here, Mr. Dondo, do you see your signature on it? It's on the right-hand screen in your own language.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recollect the information contained within this statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Give me a moment to read it, please. This is one of our daily reports that we sent to our command in Zadar, and they in turn forwarded them to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I've no further questions to ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, may this document be added to the 65 ter list of our Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May it be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1703 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document that I'd like you to look at is 65 ter 4178. It's a document dated the 31st of August of 1995, and it comes from the ECMM Regional Centre Knin. It's dated the 31st of August, 1995, and it concerns a report about an incident on the 26th of August at Orlic when there was an inspection of a house on fire, an allegation that one Croatian soldier cocked his gun, threatened one of the monitors. There was a protest about this, and it is signed by Philippe Augarde, head of the Knin Regional Centre. On the it happen right-hand side we see some handwriting. Mr. Dondo, can you see that, Karlo?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a question mark. Do you recognise whose writing that is?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I believe it is Mr. Cermak's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what is written is "Karlo?! Response." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we move down the original because -- the B/C/S. Yes, there we see the signature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this document be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything you'd like to add, Mr. Dondo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are too few letters for me to be a hundred per cent sure that the handwriting is indeed Mr. Cermak's, but I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we move a little bit so that we can see the full of the handwriting. Mr. Dondo, anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I confirm that the handwriting is Mr. Cermak's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, might this document be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D1704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1704 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document is Exhibit P1147. It is a letter dated the 8th of September, 1995. If we look at the content of the letter, it's addressed to Mr. Augarde of the European mission Regional Centre Knin from the garrison in Knin. It refers to the letter of protest dated the 31st of August, 1995, concerning an event which occurred as long ago as 26th of August on 1995, and that the letter was only received on the 6th of September, 1995. And it refers to the impermissible behaviour by a person in the uniform of a Croatian soldier and it says: "I have issued an order to the military police to investigate the case and make every attempt to discover the perpetrator." And then it refers to future cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, do you recognise this letter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how do you come to know the letter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: We, as the communications officers, forward all letters that are drafted to the United Nations, and this refers to Colonel-General, commander of the regional centre, and such communications would go through us. All the letters are written in Croatian. They are signed by General Cermak. We have them translated and hand them over to the person to whom they are addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you know if this letter is linked to the previous letter we looked at from Mr. Augarde dated the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I certainly think it is linked because the way it is phrased hints at the general's apology for the events that had happened, and it expresses the wish for the continuation of good cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you draft the response to the letter of the 31st of August? Is this a draft by you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. I'm looking at the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from the Gotovina Defence. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will have a couple of questions for Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dondo. I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Markac, and I would ask you to try to reply to them to the best of your knowledge. We are all aware that 15 years have elapsed since the events we're talking about. Mr. Dondo, since we speak the same language and our conversation has to be interpreted for the other participants to the proceedings, for the Court to be able to use them -- use it, I would like to point out that you're supposed to wait for a short while before giving your reply to enable the interpreters to do their work.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, we saw from your statements that have been tendered under numbers D1695 and D1696, that in August 1995 you were a member of the liaison department of the Croatian army for liaising with the European Union and the United Nations. You said in your statement that in that capacity you attended numerous meetings that took place with representative of the -- representatives of the international community, both as a liaison officer and as an interpreter, as you speak English. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, just very briefly, did you notice at those meetings that there is a problem with the interpreters of the UN or the European Community at the time as regards their professional qualities and with the quality of the interpretation given at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. Very often the interpreters did their work very poorly and interpreted the statements of Mr. Forand or Mr. Cermak wrongly; and thus, they changed the meaning of what was said. We would then step in as interpreters and correct it, what had been said, and sometimes we even had to go as far as to ask for the interpreters to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you understood at the time, do you think that such a low quality of interpretation provided by people hired by the European Union or the UN affect their understanding of what was going on on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I believe that may have been the case because the same interpreters also translated all letters that arrived at the UN headquarters and at the European Community headquarters. And if they were badly translated, then it is possible that they would have been misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, in your statements - we needn't repeat everything - you explain your duties and your relationship with the commander of the zone of operation and the garrison command. You mention that you sent reports to the office in Zagreb, daily reports. To which addresses did you send your reports?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: There was only one address and that was our command in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it is correct to say that you were not obliged, nor was it done in practice, to send your reports to the commander of the garrison or the commander of the army district?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, during your -- during the time that you were in Knin, there was one incident of special importance and it also has a special significance in these proceedings. I'm referring to the event at Grubori. In your statements you described your role and what you knew about that event, but let me still ask you a few questions about that. I'm now referring to paragraph 25 of your statement given in 2005. You gave it to the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Can we see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is now Exhibit D1695, paragraph 25. I apologise, 1695. You see now on the left-hand side the English version. I hope that soon we will see the Croatian version on the right-hand side. But as you speak English -- oh, here it is. Mr. Dondo, you first found out about the event at Grubori from the report submitted to you by the UNHCR representative, and the situation was very dramatic. It was on the 25th of August in the afternoon; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You instructed her to report what she had just reported to you to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, what is your understanding of the reason why that UNHCR representative came to you to inform you of the event at that village?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Because we were in fact the main point of contact for all UN issues, and they thought that everything that was happening in Knin or the surroundings should be taken care of through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a surprise to you with regard to the procedure?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It was a surprise insofar as I instructed her to turn to the police, because what she had described was a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But later on when you checked things you realised that the police, at least on that day, the 25th of August, knew nothing of that event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the next day, the 26th of August, in the morning, there was a press conference which General Cermak also attended, and then the journalists present - according to your statement - exerted a rather strong pressure on General Cermak regarding the details of the event at Grubori. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Do you mean the UN TV spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: That was a rather unpleasant situation. On the previous day they had introduced themselves to me and asked for an interview with General Cermak about the normalisation of life in Knin, and they wanted to speak about everyday topics regarding civilian life in Knin. So we didn't expect what was to come after the third sentence, we can call it an attack, regarding something that we had no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You too personally were present, weren't you, when Mr. Cermak requested information about the details of those events from the local police in Knin but never got such information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the morning of the 26th of August, there was a press conference, and after that, on the same day the so-called train of liberty came to Knin, President Tudjman was on the train and many foreign diplomats. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, Mr. Dondo, the arrival of the train of liberty on that day in Knin, what kind of consequences had it for the situation in Knin? Was the situation normal and everyday-like, or did it provoke some extraordinary situation with regard to security, police controls, et cetera? How do you remember that day, with focus on the arrival of the train?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Since the area had only recently been liberated, it is clear that addition of forces had to be employed for security -- providing security. I remember the euphoria present in Knin at the time, that's what I remember best, euphoria due to the arrival of the train and the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So priorly to that situation in Knin, you did understand that the event at Grubori was something about which you needed more information? And it was your initiative, as far as I understood, to suggest to Mr. Cermak to go to the place itself and see what had happened. Is that a correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So on the 26th of August, in the afternoon, you came to Grubori, assisted by two soldiers who escorted you to the village. At what time do you -- did you arrive at the village?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It must have been around 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then you had the opportunity to contact some of the village's inhabitants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, not right away. When we arrived there the village was deserted, and it took quite some time for the first villagers to start appearing. They were extremely frightened because they didn't know who we were, and we needed a little more time to establish normal communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is then that you understood that the villagers had been informed that on the day preceding the incident, a search of the terrain was scheduled to take place and that they, the villagers, were asked to leave the village to have -- to have the terrain ready for control?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, that was also said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your first impression on the 26th of August, in the afternoon, of the events at Grubori, what was it like and can you describe what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It is very difficult to describe in a few sentences. It was a very emotional experience because I had never before seen anything like that, murder, and -- well, I wouldn't call it torture but -- but elderly people who were paralyzed or unable to move on their own. And I must say I was astonished at the situation that I saw there, that I witnessed there. The houses had been set on fire, the livestock had been scattered, people frightened, dead bodies lying around, burnt. One body in the village centre, another on the attic of a house. People say that he was unable to move and he was dressed in pyjamas. And there was a body which didn't even look like a human body but just like a heap of ash. I wouldn't really like to continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you saw this kind of situation, human bodies, dead livestock, et cetera, you spoke to the villagers and you tried to calm them down and release the tensions. Was there anything said about burying the bodies?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: We didn't speak about burials, but we said to the villagers that we would do whatever was necessary to -- to deal with the consequences of those events and that the police would come and sanitise the ground and take all other necessary measures. So it was important to us at the time to comfort the villagers who were obviously extremely frightened because they feared that the same soldiers would return, and they didn't feel safe in their village. Although the UN bus was picking up the villagers from the surrounding villages, but these people stayed in their village and they were looking for comfort from us and that's what we wanted to give them. And this comfort wasn't to consist only in promises, but actually in deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from the village on that day, you drafted a report but before that you went to the police station and orally informed them of your observations. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the Registrar to show us document P764, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, now you're about to see a document and I will ask you to confirm whether that is the report you drafted upon returning from Grubori on the 26th of August, 1995. You said that on that day, on the 26th, in the evening, when you returned from Grubori, after -- having orally reported your observations to the police and drafted a report afterward, you say that you left a copy of that report on General Cermak's desk because he wasn't in Knin at the time but travelled to Split on the train of liberty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that what we see on the screen is this very report, and if necessary we can take a look at the second page bearing your signature?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no reference to General Cermak having travelled to Split on the train of liberty. I think the testimony so far in his statement is that General Cermak was occupied with the train arriving in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I think that we should not in the presence of the witness say what is in evidence and what is not in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're saying is that Mr. Mikulicic is misrepresenting the evidence in this respect. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the witness statement which is now D1696, paragraph 32 -- sorry, 33, line -- yes, let me check, line 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would you please check because that is in evidence. Let me just check the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 33, line 3 and 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1696 is the -- yes, is the 2009 statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I note that -- I withdraw my objections. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dondo, this is page 2 of the document, i.e., the report. Can you confirm that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 5 of the document, where you state that the villagers of Grubori were promised that sanitisation was to be carried out, most probably on the following day, on the 27th, and that the representatives of civilian structures, authorities, would come to assist them to provide them with accommodation since their houses had been destroyed. Let me ask you this, Mr. Dondo: This process of sanitisation, i.e., the provision for the dead bodies, in relation to this did you receive instructions or orders from anyone stating that you should inform the villagers of Grubori that sanitisation was to be conducted on the following day or did this come about differently?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive instructions from anyone, besides we didn't know who it was we were going to find in the village. This is out of the question. Sanitisation or human sanitisation was something that was oftentimes used at the time. Looking at the police documentation, and it was to the police that I provided a report, that was the first time I saw this term "sanitisation," and I guess that's the reason why I used it in my report. The policeman who took my report wrote -- before I wrote the report that I would write a report and that sanitisation would be conducted on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you had spent some 20-odd days in Knin prior to this incident. Is it fair to say that at the time you were confronted with the procedure of sanitisation of dead bodies which was conducted on a regular basis in that period of time? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, no, I wouldn't agree that it was conducted on a daily basis more or less, but I would agree with the fact that the term did emerge in our conversations quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly, at paragraph 8 you state that you had reported the duty service of the police administration Knin, Mr. Damir Vrkic, at 8.00 p.m., on which occasion urgent sanitisation of the village of Grubori was sought. In other words, this is what you referred to a moment ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. We are now about to come to the following day, which is the 27th, when you go to Grubori again, but this time as a guide - to put it that way - because there was a TV crew and General Cermak who went there with you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Let me correct this. Until the very last moment I was not aware of Mr. Cermak's plans because I was dealing with my duties. I didn't know about his plans at the time, just as I didn't know in general because he never informed me of his plans. I didn't know that I was supposed to join them until the very last moment, whereupon I got ready and left together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To your recollection - and we are mindful of the elapsed time - who it was that you found of the individuals, and I mean representatives of structures, organs, in the village of Grubori? Who was it who gathered in Grubori on the 27th, in other words, two days following the incident?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'd like to mention journalists who were the most numerous there, the civilian protection service, and the crime investigation police, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see members of the special police among them?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Sacic at all or to any other members of the special police about what had happened in the village of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, as a participant in these events, did you ever receive from anyone instructions or orders to the effect that the incident needed to be covered up or suppressed?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I am surprised by your question. No, I did not. I'm quite taken aback by your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the field at the time, was it ever your impression or did you receive information to the effect that measures or actions were taken at whatever level aimed at covering up the events in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: When I received the report on what had happened in Grubori from Mr. Cermak - and I received the report because I was supposed to forward it to the Red Cross which had asked for a report from us - that was the only information I had about the events at Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, in the context of your duties at the time, did you have occasion to follow what happened after the incidents in Grubori in terms of a police follow-up, investigations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, we didn't have time to deal with these matters, nor did we deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today, Mr. Dondo, if in fact you have accurate or relevant information about the actual events in Grubori, what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dondo, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Could I seek one clarification of one of your last answers. You were supposed to forward the report on what had happened in Grubori by Mr. Cermak and you said "that was the only information I had about the events in Grubori." But you had your personal observations in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did the content of the report you were supposed to forward to the Red Cross, was that in every respect consistent with your own observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be said that what happened in Grubori was, as was indeed said, a contact between enemy forces and that fire was opened from heavy weaponry upon houses. Now, the reason why civilians were killed, infirm, elderly persons, this is something I cannot fathom at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now it's not really an answer to my question you're giving. I asked you whether what you observed, whether that was consistent with the content of the report you're supposed to send to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Dondo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dondo. You testified that you speak English. Do you also read and write English well?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in -- you left the HV 1996; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: After you left the HV you were employed by Mr. Cermak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: First as a secretary and then as an operative manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you still employed by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Until when were you in such employment?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: With a brief interval, during which I was in a different company which was roughly one year up until 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you receive any retirement benefits from Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I was fired by Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When were you fired by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: In the summer of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you involved in any way in assisting the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would it not be a good idea to try to get an answer to your last question? Do you have any -- let me just check -- well, if you're fired it doesn't mean that there are necessarily no benefits remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the clarification on employed by whom should be if we're being technical about such matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the Court will understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it was for the companies, as it is stated in the statement given to the OTP. Yes. Do you -- have you any pension rights from your employment with any firm which was either owned by or directed by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that you assisted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the answer did not get reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the answer, at least as I understood it to be, was that you said that you had no pension benefits from such an employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none, from the employment with Mr. Cermak's company, no, I don't. I don't have any benefits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, isn't it correct that you assisted Mr. Cermak in his preparations towards his defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question? I'm not sure I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be more specific. Didn't you participate at the interview when Mr. Cermak was interviewed by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998, you were present at that interview, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were present throughout that interview; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that in the course of that interview from time to time you advised Mr. Cermak with regard to his responses, you provided him details of specific, you know, situations. Isn't that correct? You advised him during the course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it advice. Whenever Mr. Cermak could not recall a fact or a detail that was questionable, he would ask me; and if I knew the answer, I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, we have that transcript here in evidence, and just -- I wanted just -- I don't intend to go through all of those exchanges between you and Mr. Cermak, but I'll point you to a couple of instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. Registrar, may I have P2526, please. Mr. President, I wish to explain to the Court this -- this is the 1998 interview between Mr. Cermak and the OTP, and in the B/C/S version of the transcript you have the entire recording transcribed and which also captures the exchanges between Mr. Cermak and the witness. However, the interpreter had not interpreted the exchanges between Mr. Cermak and the witness into English, and as such the English transcript which is on record at the moment in the evidence base do not contain those exchanges. So what we -- what the Prosecution has done is we have translated those additional exchanges which has been now disclosed to the Defence. May I for ease of proceeding right now, Mr. President, be permitted to distribute hard copies of those additional translations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Distribute to whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To the Defence, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it was disclosed --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the Chamber -- it has already been disclosed and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please provide the Chamber with the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We also have hard copies if the Defence doesn't have ... Now, Mr. President, in fact these additional translations have been uploaded to e-court; however, for the time being, since we have to refer to the transcript that is on e-court vis-a-vis the additional translations, I will not call the additional translations on e-court for the time being. But we could have it linked to this exhibit later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see how this material is used, what evidence it produces, and then the technical way to deal with it is then still to be considered. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, on the screen in front of you is a record of that transcript of the interview, and in fact your -- you have been asked to identify yourself, and you say: "I'm Karolj Dondo, secretary for Mr. Cermak." And then your answer as to -- to explain your position in this interview and you say: "My participation in this interview is because of my role that I had as the secretary to Mr. Cermak and the Liaison Officer for the time that we spent in Knin." So is it correct that apart from acting as a liaison officer, you also functioned as Mr. Cermak's secretary when you were in Knin during the period --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, no, I worked as a secretary in Mr. Cermak's company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to transcript reference -- page number 15 on the English. And that would be Croatian page number 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the English, page 15, at line 26 and the Croatian version you would see, Mr. Dondo, and line 26 in front of you on the B/C/S version you were asked -- Cermak is asked a question by the investigator. The question is: "Who was your immediate superior?" And this is the portion which is not -- which has not been interpreted and is now in the additional translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if the Court and Defence could turn to page 3, Mr. President, if you could turn to page 3 of that additional translation, that is the hard copies that is with you, you can find the portion that is left out of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there is an exchange between you and Mr. Cermak. Mr. Cermak says: "To me, since I was dealing with the issues of making the town function and slowly establishing civilian authorities, and I had delegations of the international community ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is the portion that is left out of the transcript on e-court, so it's in the hard copy that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that, Ms. Mahindaratne, but I'm checking the context in e-court --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... community, with regard to all those issues, I had frequent contacts with the Office of the President, in fact Mr. Sarinic, Vesna Skare-Ozbolt, with regard to all those issues. And with regard to those other military issues, my ultimate, ultimate ... who would be my superior?" And you in fact assist Mr. Cermak, you say: "The President." And then Mr. Cermak says: "The President, no, that's not it. Wait, who could have been superior to me? Pardon. Who could have been superior to me? I did not receive orders from anybody else, but according to some hierarchy, according to the hierarchy, according to the hierarchy even the military district command could give me orders." And you again advise him: "Gotovina" -- and then there is an exchange between you and Mr. Cermak which has not been captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just turn the page so our clients could follow along in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could move to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So isn't it correct, Mr. Dondo, that you, in fact, and I could really take you through several such exchanges between you and Mr. Cermak -- you in fact were advising Mr. Cermak on what responses he should provide to the investigators in the course of that interview; isn't that correct? It is right here on record.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't recall this. It was a long time ago. I don't remember the details, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You may not remember the details, Mr. Dondo, but this is on record. In fact, the videotape is in evidence and this is just a mere transcript of what is on the videotape. So do you agree that you, in fact, assisted Mr. Cermak in the course of that interview with regard to what responses he should provide to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I can't agree with you before I've read the transcript. I am not familiar with it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. We could -- actually later on in relation to certain other matters I will go to some of these exchanges. Now, just one other question. As the liaison officer, apart from acting as an intermediary between the international organisations and Mr. -- and the Croatian authorities, did you also function as an intermediary between the Croatian authorities themselves, for example, did you function as an intermediary between Mr. Cermak and the civilian police or Mr. Cermak and the military police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No. We were intermediaries between Mr. Cermak and any other commander, be it Mr. Gotovina, the commander of Sector South to whom we were subordinated at one point, and the international community, i.e., the UN and the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cermak use the liaison officers at all to convey any instructions either to the civilian police or the military police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Would this be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a good time for the break, but could I first inquire with you -- let's focus on page 15 of the English because you indicate in your hard copy where to find what. Now I see on the third page of this hard copy you gave to us reference is made to the English translation page 15, line 11; then page 15, line 12; and then in the English translation page 16, line 13, which comes a bit as a surprise in view of what we later find, that is, English translation page 15, line 27. Now, I see that apart from whether it makes any sense to make a distinction between page 15, lines 11, 12, and 13, I find there in our English version translation interpreted by conversation in Croatian between Ivan Cermak and Karolj Dondo. So that explains clearly what we find there. However, on page 15, line 27, I do not see any indication as to any conversation which was apparently not translated. So I'm just wondering as to how complete the English version is in stating that there is a missing portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is not, Mr. President. In fact, you are correct. The English transcript, which is now in the evidence base, does not at each point where there is an exchange missing, does not in fact indicate that there is an exchange missing. What the language assistants did was in fact compared the Croatian version and the English version, practically line to line, and that's how they gathered that there was certain portions missing in the English transcript, and hence the indication as to where exactly the missing portions should fit in the English transcript. But unfortunately, on the English transcript itself, it is in the record, everywhere it doesn't report that there is an exchange missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I find apparently after page 15, line 27, I find -- well, five to six, if not seven lines untranslated without any trace in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. From the comparison, the portion that is missing that is -- which should be at line 27 and then the rest that is recorded should really add on to that, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the reference to page 16, line 13, on that same page, is that just a mistake or is it -- because I -- it gives me the impression, but I've seen it only for a few seconds, that it's all chronologically --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is a mistake, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a mistake. That should be page 15 then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be page 15. I'll have that corrected on what will be uploaded and a link to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, let me take you to the incident in Grubori, since we just discussed about that. Now, in your -- in the statement you made to the OTP in 2005, and that is D1695, this is what you say. If you want to follow it on the hard copy --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: [In English] I would like it, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D1695 and move to page 9 of the English. It's paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while the Croatian is coming up, I will -- let me just read what you've stated. You say: "I think the first I knew was when the UNHCR representative came to us very upset. She was dramatising everything and saying that assistance should be sent immediately because people were being killed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... because people were being killed and houses were being burnt. I think she was accompanied by two others from the same organisation." You have, in fact, made an amendment to paragraph 25 with regard to that specific item of evidence, and that is at paragraph 30 of your 2009 statement made to the Defence, that's D1696, and this is what you say there: "We received the first information about the incident in the village of Grubori on the same day that it happened, at around 1600 hours. The lady who arrived at our Office for Cooperation was most likely a member of the UN civil affairs. She told us that there were shots fired and that houses were burning in Grubori." And the last three lines of paragraph 30 you say: "At that time we did not know that people had been killed, nor did we know in the morning of the next day, 26 August 1995 ..." Now, my question to you is: In your statement to the OTP you said that the first information that you received was that people were being killed and houses were being burnt; but in 2009 when you spoke to the Defence, you said that the first report was that houses were being burnt and shots were fired, that there was no reference to people being killed. Now, what was the basis for that amendment? Why in 2009 did you think that you had not received information about people being killed in that first report?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that the first report that I gave to the OTP on the date stated - I can't see it here now but I think it was in 1996 if I'm not mistaken - that report was drafted in a specific manner, as it were, because I was invited by the OTP asking me whether I could come to testify on the following day about my stay at Knin and everything that had happened, so without any preparation and without being reminded or reminding myself of everything that had happened in the past ten years. Here it is even said that she dramatised. Well, that may be overstating it a bit, but she was certainly very upset. This may be due to a translation error. The reason was that I wasn't prepared for the first meeting and wasn't able to go into the details of the events as I wasn't prepared, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So are you saying that due to the fact that you were not prepared your statement to the effect -- that you made a mistake and that's why you said that your -- the first information you received it was mentioned that people were being killed. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It is possible that the first time around I said that people were being killed and that that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what kind of preparations did you take before your to -- your state -- interview with the Defence, which made you remember the incident much better than in 2005?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Among other things, the reports that we wrote and other materials were read. We sent reports to our command, to our headquarters, about all the details. So that was -- that was something that could remind me of whether or not I really did mention that people were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What report or what material did you read prior to your interview with the Defence which reminded you that you didn't in fact say -- that you did not receive that information in that first report you received from the international monitors about the Grubori event? What is it that you read?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but it was much material. Among other things, my first statement that I gave to the OTP; but once you have time to think about it more thoroughly things start looking somewhat different. But it is a fact that people had been killed. So in my case, it isn't so important what I first said. And whether or not she really said to me on that occasion is -- I don't consider relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, could you refrain from giving your opinion on relevance and importance of matters that are a part of the questions that are put to you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you just said that you read much material prior to your interview -- the statement you gave to the Defence. Who provided you with that material?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that material was?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It consisted of reports and of documents that were exchanged between the UN and the garrison command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the reports, were they also reports going between the UN and Mr. Cermak or were they other reports?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak and the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "garrison command"? What were --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak as the commander of the garrison, so he was commander of the garrison, and the UN and the EC on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you read any statements of witnesses in the -- who have testified in these proceedings or who are yet to testify?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you read any transcripts of any testimony?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you follow the proceedings before this Trial Chamber on TV?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Sometimes I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall whose testimony did you follow?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you watch the testimony of Mr. Alun Roberts?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Edward Flynn?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Dondo, now of the reports that you read, what is the report or what were the reports that you read which provided you of a clear memory of what happened on the 25th as to exactly what information you received from the UN monitors about the incident which you didn't have in 2005 when you spoke with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Those are mostly the reports that we sent to headquarters in Zagreb. We collected our reports daily and sent them to the command in Zagreb, and they kept a register of the evidence -- of the events that were taking place at Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be specific as to what was the report you read that made you remember that in that first report that you received from the international monitors they had not mentioned that people were being killed? I'm asking you for the specific -- what is the basis for you to make that amendment in 2009?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also mentioned that -- the term "dramatising," you say "she was dramatising everything and saying that assistance should be sent immediately ..." Now, you said dramatising may be an overstatement. Mr. Dondo, we had Mr. Roberts who testified in these proceedings, who in fact specifically testified about your reactions when that first report was made to you. And this is -- for the record I'm referring to P675, paragraph 15 and 16. This is what he said about your reactions: "We decided to go direct to the office of General Cermak in Knin to report what we saw. At the lobby of the building the assistant or main Liaison Officer to General Cermak came down to meet us, Dondo. We asked if the Croatian authorities knew of anything special happening in Plavno? He listened, but seemed unaware. My colleagues, EJ Flynn of HRATS, Maria Teresa Mauro of Humanitarian Affairs, and Benny Otim, head of UNHCR office at Sector HQ, described what we saw in Plavno and Grubori. They urged that because this had just happened and houses were still burning that the Croatian authorities act quickly, go to Grubori, and begin an investigation. In the middle of the conversation I thought it odd that the Liaison Officer asked why I had been in Plavno?" Is that correct, Mr. Dondo, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "I replied because I had been at the same meeting as the UN press officer. The moment was overtaken by the urging of my UN colleagues for quick response. I recall that they asked to receive a report and follow-up and that he inform General Cermak. My thoughts were that I did not sense any great urgency by the Liaison Officer. I did not hear him say, 'We will contact you on what we find' or why the police did not arrive for the meeting. He seemed unhappy with the UN insisting and that the UN press officer was present." Now, in your statement to the OTP you used the term that the UNHCR representative came to you very upset and that she was dramatising everything. Now, did you feel at the time that the reaction from the international monitors was unwarranted in the given circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It is possible because it had happened on several occasions that the United Nations would blow some things out of proportion, and subsequently it became clear that they weren't really as bad as that and that very little or nothing had happened in reality. We were able to witness such instances. So, yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you didn't think at the time that the matter warranted urgent intervention at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that the issue must be investigated, but that it was also possible that the accounts were exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is that upon receipt of that information from the international monitors, you immediately informed Mr. Cermak and that Mr. Cermak then called the civilian police and did not receive any information from them. And then you also go on to say, in your statement to the OTP, that you also believed that Mr. Cermak contacted the military police and did not receive from the military police either any information on the matter. Now, apart from contacting the civilian police and the military police and asking them what they knew about the matter, did General Cermak contact anyone else on the 25th regarding this incident?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't know that, not in my presence anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, apart from calling them and asking them what information they had on the matter, did General Cermak instruct the civilian police to immediately go to the area, go to Plavno, Grubori, and investigate the matter or to verify if the report was accurate?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any authority to give instructions to the police. He simply inquired whether they were aware of what was going on; and if not, that they should go there and check things because we had information from the UN that something was going on or had gone on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on the 25th, after that initial telephone call, did Mr. Cermak at any time discuss this incident with you or inform you of any other information he had received about the event in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I asked him several times whether he knew anything about it, and every time the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the case on the 26th August also, the next day, following day, at any time, to your knowledge, had General Cermak received any information on this incident as to how it had happened or any other information?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Since Mr. Cermak mentioned some details on UN TV, details about another case, I'm sure that he had received information from somebody, albeit false, deliberately or not. But I think that Mr. Cermak was not familiar with this case before he received my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then when you say "he was not familiar with this case before he received my report," you're referring to your report that you compiled after your visit to Grubori on the 26th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if I could take you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could we seek clarification from that "Mr. Cermak mentioned some details on UN TV, details about another case," what other case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember exactly, but if we can see the video, which would be a good thing because the video is short, so then everything will become clear. The UN TV report I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would there be any way of perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I intend to, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to show to the witness and then to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, I wasn't planning to show -- play the video, but I thought I will read the transcript. Just playing the video might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if the witness says that false information is contained in the video, it might be in portions that you're not putting to him. And I would like to have an opportunity to -- for a better assessment --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the probative value his answer in this respect. Is there any way that, for example, during one of the breaks that we could give an opportunity to the witness to watch the video and then to tell us exactly what information came from what other case and to what extent it was false?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If there is time, actually, I could even play it in court. But since playing the entire thing might take time, perhaps in the break as you suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have any recollection on how long the video exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not that long, Your Honour. It might help the witness, since we're on this point now and it's something he has asked for, for the court to facilitate that. It's on the OTP's list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I leave it to the parties whether -- if we would ask the witness to look at it and then answer questions, then there might be a need to play parts of it again. I mean, I -- it might be good for us as well to watch it again so to know exactly what it was. "Not long" is a relative --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Under ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could play it, Mr. President. I think it would be best if I do that, just after a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, I will play that video for you, but before that I just want to take you to your 2009 statement, that is D1696. In paragraph 39 -- 31, I'm sorry, this is what you say, you say: "I organised a meeting with Mr. Cermak and the UN TV crew. Mr. Cermak was surprised by the questions asked by the TV crew because we did not know what had happened in Grubori. Mr. Cermak only had the information he had received from me, and he found out from the TV crew that murders had taken place in the village of Grubori. I did not have any information and I was pressured by the UN, as they asked every half an hour if there was any new information. The pressure from the UN and media representatives on Mr. Cermak was great. They requested concrete information from him on the incidents that had taken place. "That afternoon President Tudjman was arriving in Knin with the freedom train. Before Mr. Cermak went to await for the arrival of the president, I asked him if he had any new information from the civil police or anyone else. He told me that he had not received any information and that he still did not know anything about what happened in Grubori."
