So according to your testimony, Mr. Cermak didn't know any information whatsoever about the Grubori incident, even in the afternoon of 26th August; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I was able to conclude from the several conversations I had with him, no, he didn't have any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, I think the witness clearly testified that Mr. Cermak did not know anything beyond what this witness had told him on the basis of the information he had received. And you are putting the question in a rather absolute way, no knowledge at all, but that's of course not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he did not receive any additional information, that's -- I take it that's the gist of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answers Mr. Cermak gave were the same on the day before and on the day he took the train; in other words, that he had no information as to what had transpired over there. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your conclusion was that because he gave the same answers on the second day that he had not received any additional information. You could not conclude from what he said that he had received any further information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, may I take it, is your answer? Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, we will play that video, since you wish to see it. This is P504, but we'll play the video -- the transcript is on e-court on P504. We'll play the video which is V000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the transcript been provided to the booths?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think the whole video has been played before. I will just confer with Mr. Registrar whether we could adopt the same transcript if we are not doing anything else than to look at this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the consent of the parties and the transcript not having been distributed and the transcript already being in evidence, I suggest that we do not make a great effort to have it on the record again. The witness is able to hear it in the original language, and from what I remember it was subtitled, the English was subtitled. So therefore, there's no need at this moment to have it translated again. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could have V000-1241.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop here? Here General Cermak states that a member of the Serb army was taken prisoner and that a Croatian soldier was found with his hands tied behind his back with wire, which is absolutely inconsistent with the situation as we found it in Grubori. Since before saying that, he clearly and accurately states what the operation was about, where, and what its scope was but then proceeded to give completely inaccurate information as to the consequences and the effects of the operation shows that he did receive information about the events from someone. However, the information happened to be completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we move on? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there still was the question, he was mixing up another case. Where is that case and what was that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I would kindly ask the Defence to assist me in that. I think it was an event that took place several days earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, if you know, tell us; if you don't know, then it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, who did give this false information to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he was given any false information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you say what he said was inconsistent with the situation you had found in Grubori, that -- that you give an explanation for that but you have no factual basis for such an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I don't have to play the video any further, unless the Trial Chamber would want -- would wish the rest of the video footage to be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your focus was on what Mr. Cermak during this interview gave as information, and we -- I think we further explored one of the previous answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber feels no need to further play the video, but if any of the other parties for contextualisation would need it, we would hear from them. Ms. Mahindaratne, it remains silent so therefore please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, this interview took place early on 26th August, isn't it, in the morning of 26th August?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you the person who interpreted for Mr. Cermak at -- in the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Generally when you were around, wasn't it you who interpreted for Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Generally speaking, there were always two of us. When we attended meetings with General Cermak, there would be liaison officers, one of whom would follow the conversation and the other would interpret simultaneously. It was important to follow the conversation in order to make sure that the other side was being accurately interpreted as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is that on the afternoon -- in the afternoon of 26th August, when you found out that Mr. Cermak had not received any information from the police regarding the incident, you proposed to Mr. Cermak that you should travel to Grubori to investigate the matter. Now, as a liaison officer, why did you take it upon yourself to conduct such a mission? That's not within your normal functions as a liaison officer. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It does fall within our remit. If there are matters that are unclear and the UN seeks a response on that matter and we are unable to obtain it from the authorities, we have the duty to go out into the field ourselves and investigate the matter, whilst of course asking for the assistance of advice from an officer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, the interpreter has not heard the last part of your answer. Could you repeat the last part of your answer. Is it -- "... whilst of course asking for the assistance of advice from an officer ..." and you didn't complete the sentence.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: From an officer charged with the area of responsibility where the liaison officer is active.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, up until that time, didn't Mr. Cermak instruct anybody to go to Grubori to investigate the matter and to at least find out the accuracy of the reports he had received?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you travelled to Grubori on the 27th August -- I'm sorry, 26th August, had the civilian police or an investigative judge or any other authority been to civilian -- to Grubori to investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As a liaison officer, did you find that to be a matter of concern and did you report that matter to anybody in authority, that the civilian police even by the next day had not been to Grubori to investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It was a problematic issue by all accounts. The first thing I did upon my return was go to the civilian police to report the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what exactly did you inform the police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I told them what I saw and the extent of that can be found in my written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you inquire from the civilian police as to why the police had not gone to Grubori to investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, I don't have that sort of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as a liaison officer -- now you just said that you even had the authority to go to the field to investigate with the assistance of relevant -- an officer of the relevant authority to find out what's going on. Were you not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I would just object to the word "investigate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness used that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Certainly not in Croatian language, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll check what he said, and let me first try to find -- it was -- we'll check that. I have to find it. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is Your Honour thinking of page 51, line 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be. Yes. The witness there said: "We have the duty to go out into the field ourselves and investigate the matter." Mr. Mikulicic, if you say he didn't use the word "investigate" in Croatian, then we'll have to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that will be my proposal, Your Honour, because the word "investigate" is quite official term and it obviously has some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we just check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say that's not what he said, then we'll have to seek clarification what was said on -- in the original language on page 51, line 10. Let's proceed for the time being. Perhaps the witness remembers what word he used -- of course we can verify that at a later stage, where you said you had a duty to go into the field where matters were unclear and investigate. If you remember what word you used, please tell us so that we would know immediately; and otherwise, we'll check it because there's audio recording -- yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't remember which particular word I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed at the time as matters stand now on the basis of the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you said as a liaison officer you had even the authority to go to the field and investigate matters. Is it your position that you don't, then, have authority to even request an investigation from the police or even ask them as to why they had not investigated into a matter where you yourself saw five civilians had been killed and houses burnt?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes. I was a soldier and that was the civilian police. I have no powers over them. I can ask them as a private individual why it was that they didn't go up there and investigate, but they don't have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Cermak that even on 26th when you went to Grubori that the civilian police had not been there to investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I didn't know that. We presumed, since we did not receive a reply from anyone, neither the civilian nor the military police, about what had transpired there -- we presumed that nobody had been there. That was the main reason why I went there to begin with. We didn't know if anyone had been there, but we presumed that no one had since we did not receive a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. But then you said that you went to Grubori on the 26th, and even when you went to Grubori, the police had not been there to conduct an investigation. So your presumption was confirmed upon your visit to Grubori. So upon that, did you not think it would be appropriate to report to somebody that in a serious matter such as this the civilian police had not initiated an investigation even after 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, before the witness answers the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before he answers. Yes, an objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the premise of the question because there is evidence in this case that indicates otherwise in the Knin police log-book recorded by the chief of the local police, Knin police, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- will recollect that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where we have two entries, I think, on the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and there is an earlier entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, while --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I know that -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- nevertheless, yes, if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I intend to, in fact, call that -- the log-book. In fact, Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- should know that I provided the notice of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your question was whether the assumption or presumption was confirmed during the visit. Now that we are talking about the perception of this witness, Mr. Kay, I think that's what we are talking about at this moment so we can ask him about this, and then what is to be found in other documents and on what basis is then still a matter to be seen. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please phrase your question in such a way that Mr. Kay has no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, when you visited Grubori it was confirmed to you that the civilian police had not been to Grubori on the 26th. Did you consider that relevant enough to inform Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Cermak, I also informed the civilian police. Other than that, I simply don't understand your question. You'll have to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Cermak upon your return from Grubori on the 26th or even 27th morning before you went with Mr. Cermak to Grubori again, that when you went to Grubori that you found the civilian police had not been to Grubori to investigate this crime, did you inform Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, because I didn't see Mr. Cermak until the following day when we set out for Grubori again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just call up -- since it's just been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have D57, please. That's the Knin police log-book. And if we could move to in the English page 59 and the Croatian version page 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At entry number 193 there's a report from the commander of the police station, Milos Mihic. The report recalls -- it says report on a body. "He reported verbally that information had been received that in Plavno village, Grubori hamlet, on 25th August 1995, two male bodies were found; Milos Grubar, born 1915, and Jovan Grubar, 60 years of age." And in the "action" columns it says: "It was agreed with Chief Cedo Romanic that an on-site investigation would be conducted in the morning of 27th August 1995. Civilian protection went to the scene at 1100 hours on 27 August 1995, and removed the bodies." Now, this entry in fact confirms that on the 26th the police had not been to Grubori to investigate the matter, so your observation was correct, Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we are on this report if we could move to page 61 of the English version and page 63 of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On the same day, that is the 26th, you have made a report to the police at 2000 hours. This is entry number 197. Your report is: "In Plavno village, Grubori hamlet, there are five bodies of men and women who were killed during military and police Operation Storm. "Information on this will be subsequently passed on to civilian protection officers for hygiene and sanitation measures." Now, in relation to this in paragraph 33 of your 2009 statement, that is the statement made to the Defence, you had been shown this entry and you say -- actually, you have been shown a corresponding document which contains the same entry, that is D1393, which is the log-book for the Knin police administration. You say: "I can see that it is stated that the cause of death of those people was Operation Storm. I must say that I did not mention Operation Storm in my report, nor was the incident in Grubori connected with Operation Storm." Now, how do you know that, that these deaths as to whether it was conducted with Operation Storm or what it was connected with? How do you know that in the first place, since you told today in your testimony that even today you don't know what really happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I know because I learned as much in the conversations with the villagers of that village, and they told me that the incident had taken place on the previous day and they told me what happened and how. They said when it happened, and not only they, it was also stated in the UN reports. And according to all the reports, the incident had nothing to do with Operation Storm. And most importantly -- or rather, the most important thing were the statements of the villagers from that village who were filled with fear and emotionally overwhelmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, do you consider the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you would not mind. You said that -- one second, please. You said it was also stated in the UN reports. Which reports are you referring to exactly as being available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The oral reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The oral report of which you said it might have been an exaggeration, that one, the Italian lady, so to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and reports that came in later from various sides such as from the Red Cross and others. The first report I received I considered relatively exaggerated, but when we saw that reports were coming in more frequently from various parties, we understood how serious the situation was and we concluded that something serious was going on and that concrete measures had to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to follow your evidence. You say the entry in the police log is wrong because you did not mention Operation Storm, and then you explain to us why this was wrong anyhow. So that's -- did you know at that time when you reported to the police at -- that it was not Operation Storm, because that, I think, is what Ms. Mahindaratne asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he asked me as much and I clearly replied that I knew this wasn't due to Operation Storm. It must have been an omission or an error made by the police officer who entered that into the log, inadvertently or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say, "I knew that it was not linked to Operation Storm," referring to UN reports, the only report available at that point in time to you was the oral report, whatever confirming reports there may have been at a later stage. But at that moment the only source you had was the UN oral report, people coming to you including the Italian lady who was quite upset. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This police report was written after I had returned from Grubori, so after I had seen what I had seen. And after having a conversation, after talking to the villagers of that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the only UN report you had available at that moment -- I was just exploring what reports apart from your own observations were there at the time. You had no UN reports in addition to what was reported orally to you by - I again say - the Italian lady being quite upset. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, when you say "Operation Storm," are you referring just to the operation -- the initial attack from -- which took place from 4th to 8th or 9th August, or do you consider the clearing operations that were carried out after Operation Storm, the initial attack was completed, as also part of an operation? Or do you consider it as not being linked to Operation Storm? I'm just trying to understand your evidence.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I repeat once more. I never stated that what happened at the village of Grubori, at Plavno, was linked to Operation Storm. I never said as much to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me ask you this way: When you left Grubori after your own investigations were conducted on 26th, did you know that the incident had occurred in the course of a clearing operation or a mop-up operation that had been conducted by the special police or the military?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you mention that fact to the police when you made your report?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have P764, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, this is the report you compiled after your visit, and if you could just focus on paragraph 1. You refer to: "... visible evidence of yesterday's clearing operation ..." and you clarify what that evidence is: "... possessions strewn about houses and outside, several houses had been set on fire, and livestock were wandering without supervision ..." And my question is: The reference from you, you consider that evidence as evidence of the clearing operation from the previous day, is that based on your previous recollections of how a place looked like after a clearing operation that were being conducted during this period?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the fact that you saw possessions strewn about houses and outside, several houses being burnt and livestock wandering around as evidence of the previous day's clearing operation. Now, is that how a place looked like after the clearing operation? Is that because you considered that as evidence of a clearing operation. My question to you is: Is that based on your recollection of how a place generally looked like after a clearing operation?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I'm still utterly unclear about this. This -- it makes no sense to me to say that the place looked like one in which a mop-up operation had taken place because houses had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to your own report, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I -- maybe I can assist. I'm told the interpretation is unclear as to what the intent of my learned friend's questions are, which may be why there appears to be a problem. Perhaps there could be some consideration in the language that is being used. I'll say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now is there any specific portion? If you could point us at pages and lines where the confusion may arise so that we could invite Ms. Mahindaratne to ask the same but perhaps in a -- in a new phrasing, not necessarily because the phrasing is wrong, but it may have caused some -- I'm not saying it did, but it may have caused some confusion in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could try rephrasing, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's then first try to find out the exact portion is which may have caused the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if I can assist my learned friends. I'm told that the difficulty comes at page 61, line 23 and 24, the last question there after the previous text is unclear as to what is meant. It might be fine in the English -- it might be fine in the English language, but I'm told that there is a problem in this -- expressing it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps paraphrase in such a way that the minimum -- that the risk of confusion in translation will be minimal. I'm not saying that any mistake was made, but let's try to see whether we can proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll try, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, could you please read the first paragraph where you recall -- you say -- you refer to the village and hamlets you say: "... with visible evidence of yesterday's clearing operation ..." And then you clarify it further: "... possessions strewn about houses and outside, several houses had been set on fire, and livestock were wandering without supervision ..." Now, why did you consider that evidence as evidence of a clearing operation?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: So the first paragraph in my report does not refer to the Grubori hamlet. I only mention it in the second paragraph. But indeed, when an army conducts a mop-up operation and passes through a village, it mostly enters houses to check them and possibly throws things around and opens barns so that the livestock strays. But the first paragraph does not imply that the mop-up operation is the cause of the incident in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this report you refer to the five bodies you observed. Now, were there any weapons near any of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there weapons anywhere in the village on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now on 27th August, that is the day after, you accompanied General Cermak to Grubori. Did you meet him before departing to Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say did I meet him? Whether we had a meeting or -- I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah, did you have a meeting or did you have even a brief -- did you have an informal discussion?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I didn't even know that our travel to Grubori would be organised in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So who asked you to accompany General Cermak? Did he ask you himself or did someone else instruct you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: It was General Cermak in person immediately before departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At the time were you in your office?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did Mr. Cermak contact you from his office?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I suppose so, but I know that everybody was ready to leave when I was told that we were going to Grubori again. So the journalists and everybody were already prepared, so I was quite surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how did you travel? Did you travel with Mr. Cermak in his vehicle or did you travel in different vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. We had vehicles of our own, and I believe that I went in my own vehicle but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cermak -- according to your testimony, Mr. Cermak was aware that you were going to Grubori on the 26th. In fact, he provided you with the escort. So did he at any time before he -- the group departed to Grubori or perhaps in the course of it or even in Grubori discuss your report with you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did he at least ask you - you know, he knew that you had been to Grubori the day before - as to what you saw, whether the reports from the international monitors were accurate? Didn't he at least make an informal inquiry from you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you knew that you -- the group was going to Grubori and you were aware that the journalists were going to be there. Didn't you think it appropriate to discuss or tell General Cermak about what you had seen the day before?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I repeat that I didn't know we would go to Grubori and the journalists would be there. I didn't know until the very last moment, until departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But at the time you got into your vehicles, you would have known where you were heading; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At least didn't you think it would be prudent to discuss, if you didn't have the opportunity to discuss on the way at least just as you get to Grubori, with General Cermak as to what you had seen before, what you had learnt?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: If I wasn't asked any questions, I wasn't in the position to suggest anything to the general or say anything to him. In the army you speak when you're spoken to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you -- your testimony is that your report, P764, after you compiled it you left it on General Cermak's table since he was not in on 26th evening. Now, generally when he's not available, is that the way reports are left for him, it's left on his table, is it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No, it isn't usual. But in this specific case, knowing the urgency and the importance of that situation for him, knowing what had happened, it was important for both the Croatian and the international public, I saw to it that it be -- that it arrive to his office as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And have you had previous instances where you left reports on his desk for him where it has reached him?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know of any instances previously where reports left for him on his table had not reached him, where he had inquired?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak received all the reports he had asked for, at least from our office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could I ask -- he asked specifically for this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's try to get to the core which seems to be at least what Ms. Mahindaratne is interested to know and what apparently creates some confusion with her. I think she's pointing at several elements in your answers. The first one is that what Mr. Cermak said during the press conference on the morning of the 26th was apparently based on, as you said, wrong information. Now, you were going to Grubori in the afternoon of the 26th and you find a situation which is quite different from what Mr. Cermak described at the press conference. You're going to Grubori. You are aware that there's a lot of media present, and what Ms. Mahindaratne has apparently difficulties in understanding is that you had not at one moment communicated with Mr. Cermak to the extent of: Are you aware that what I find yesterday and what I reported to you in a report which I left on your desk is quite different from what you told the press yesterday morning, shouldn't we be -- shouldn't we try to find out what happened? That's apparently what's bothering Ms. Mahindaratne. She has great difficulties in understanding why despite these rather big discrepancies that not a word was said about that, with the only explanation: If you're not asked anything in the military, you don't speak. Do you have an answer to what seems to be the core of the many questions that were put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say my opinion, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, opinion is your own behaviour, so you can tell us what may have been at the basis of that behaviour or what you observed on the part of Mr. Cermak. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that Mr. Cermak, upon receiving my report, communicated with the special police forces and gave them an account of what I stated in my report and asked them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm not asking you to speculate on what you do not know, which -- but what may have been done by Mr. Cermak. The question was focussing about the absence of whatever communication, even communication like, "Have you found my report?" That's what I'm seeking your comment on, not on what Mr. Cermak may have done and of which you are not aware and on which you want to give your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is that until halfway to Grubori, General Cermak had my report in his hands and he was reading it. And he was comparing the accounts in my report to the situation on the ground. After some time, Mr. Sacic from the special police and others turned up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. I'd like to hear about Mr. Sacic in a second. You said: "... until halfway to Grubori, General Cermak had my report in his hands ..." Where was that that you saw him having your report in his hands? Was he still in the car? Was he out of the car? Where were you and what did you exactly see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him while we were waiting for Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic, and I saw him in the village of Grubori when we got there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "we were waiting," I might have missed it in your statement. Where exactly were you waiting for Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic? That is, in your statement it only says "on the way there," but where was that? Was he still in his car? Were you waiting out of the cars? Were you not yet in Grubori? If not, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't describe exactly the place where we were. We were waiting for them halfway through. I know that the journalists who were there as well got out of the car and walked about. The wait certainly lasted for a good half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got out of your car as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak got out of his car as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you see him reading out of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him holding my report in his hands, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at what distance were you from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say that I was practically by his side, in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did not exchange one word whatsoever on what was found in the report? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm also looking at the clock. We'll have a break first and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before we continue I have one, perhaps two, follow-up questions. Mr. Dondo, you just told us that you were standing next to Mr. Cermak when you were waiting for the others halfway when you went out of your car. Were you close enough to see that it was actually your report that he was reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you see the text? Is that how you could establish that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I even heard him reading the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was reading it aloud? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is a kind of communication, as a matter of fact, isn't it, if you start reading aloud if someone is standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been trying to explain this earlier on but it seems that we had problems communicating. When I, as a liaison officer, write a report for my commander, the matter is closed there. There is no need for further communication because there is no need for Mr. Cermak to have any doubts about my report. Communication would be warranted at the point where he had reasons to suspect what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, before I go on to what happened on the 27th I could now ask you one question with regard to the 26th. Now your testimony is that by 26th, the police had not gone to Grubori to investigate the matter, which was in fact confirmed by the Knin log-book, D57, which records the police as going to Grubori on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and -- to assist my learned friend, I hope it's taken in the right spirit, it may be some propositions are put as evidence which are not, in fact, the evidence, transcript page 5715 of the 3rd of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you could please check that source. I take it that you will be able to find that page rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to avoid delay I will just rephrase my question if that's a problematic area. I will just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether then any objection remains or whether -- I'll -- meanwhile I'll check the source given by Mr. Kay at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it might be important background information behind the question that should be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Does that assist Your Honour on the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am -- just arrived now on the right page and I take it that Ms. Mahindaratne will check it as well. And you're referring to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 5715, transcript 3rd of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but any specific line because I've got that -- I'll read then the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have that, but if Your Honour sees the word: "At 1500 hours on the 26th" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that proposition really changes -- has an impact on my question because clearly there is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you are talking about the result, whereas Mr. Kay may have on his mind efforts. If you could please keep that in mind in phrasing your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, now your testimony is that when you went to Grubori onto 26th, at the time you went, the police had not been to the village of Grubori to investigate the matter. Now, I want to, on that point, show you -- to go back to what Mr. Cermak told the UN TV on 26th morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have D504 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm going to just read that portion of the transcript, Mr. Dondo, so that we don't waste time looking at the video again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, P504, Mr. Registrar. My apologies. And on the English if we could go to the next page. If we could go to page 2 of the English and also the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, the interviewer asks Mr. Cermak this question: "Yesterday, your office was informed of this and you promised to take immediate action. However, the Croatian police went to the local larger village but they haven't yet been to the village where the burning took place. Why can the Croatian authorities not go and help people who are still in that village, with the village burning and two corpses in two houses?" And General Cermak responds as follows: "Again, I don't know where the gentlemen has this information from about two civilians killed, and it's not true that the Croatian civilian authorities cannot get to that village. The Croatian civilian authorities got to this village, looked after the people, organised humanitarian assistance for them and other assistance they need, and people stayed in their houses. "General, I don't wish to contradict. We were there this morning. There has been no Croatian police presence in that village. There are five women there and there are two corpses, and after reporting it here again [sic], no one has been to help these people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My text reads "yesterday" instead of again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you were present at this interview, in the morning, when General Cermak made this statement to the journalist, the reporters. Then you went to Grubori and found out for yourself that the civilian police had not been to Grubori. Didn't you consider it necessary to inform General Cermak that what he had told the UN TV crew in the morning was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: This must be a misunderstanding. How could I have known that it was inaccurate when I went there the day after? That must be a mistake of some sort. I went there the day after. The interview took place in the morning and I went to Grubori on the same day, in the evening, so I don't understand your question. I'm sorry. You'll have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You probably did not understand my question. My question was: You were present when this interview was given in the morning?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That evening you went to Grubori and found out for yourself that the police had not been to Grubori to investigate. Now, at that point did you not consider it relevant or important to let General Cermak know that the statement he made to the UN TV in the morning was inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Even if I had, I could not have done it, I could not have informed him of it because he was not there. He was in Split. He was not in his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now do you agree with me that based on your own findings that General Markac's statement to the UN TV crew on 26 July morning about the police having gone to Grubori and helping the people is false?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Markac?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter. I'm grateful to my learned friend Mr. Cayley. It doesn't say "police." It says "civilian authorities." So I think we have to be careful about terminology when we do use headings in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you then exclude civilian police from civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not excluding anything myself. I'm saying the proposition of the question if it's being founded on as to whether the statement is false, that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please rephrase your question, giving the exact wording of what was said by Mr. Cermak during his interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, can you respond to my question? Now, based on your own findings consequent to your visit to Grubori in the evening of 26 August, do you agree with me that General Cermak's statement or interview given to UN TV crew in the morning of 26, where he says that "... already civilian authorities had been to Grubori and had helped the people ..." is an inaccurate statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going to the 26th -- 27th August, to the questions from the Bench, you mentioned that you were standing right by General Cermak. I want to show you a -- play the video interview where General Cermak gave to the reporter Nadja Surijak [phoen]. Have you seen that video since the 27th?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is P2386. Mr. President, I'll play the video on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been played before, so we don't -- you have not distributed the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's only a small portion that I'm going to play [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A small portion, then perhaps we follow the usual procedure, which is that one interpreter follows whether the words spoken are reflected in the text and the other interpreter being able to interpret the text as written. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are in the village of Grubori, one of the Chetnik strongholds, which during the operation of cleaning the area, you see, there was the fighting between the special units of MUP and the remaining Chetnik groups. There was some ten remaining terrorists who put up resistance. At that point in time the village was torched. During the operation itself, three members of the Chetnik groups and two civilians got killed. I came personally to the village of Grubori to see the development of the operation and I brought along the whole crew with me to let the facts be known, to let the truth be known, and not to have Croatia accused again of deliberate burnings, deliberate killings, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you testified -- you answered to questions from the Bench that on the way General Cermak was reading your report and, in fact, even after he alighted from his vehicle, he was reading your report aloud. Now, we just saw General Cermak making a statement and he says that -- he refers to an operation and he says "during the operation itself, three members of the Chetnik group and two civilians got killed," which is inconsistent to what you have reported. Now, are you able to reconcile what Mr. Cermak is saying on record here, in Grubori, on the 27th, while you are also there with your report, with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Can the interpreter repeat the bit about reconcile. I didn't understand. Can the interpreter repeat that bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can ask Ms. Mahindaratne to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rephrase her question. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Dondo, that based on your own findings, based on what you yourself reported to General Cermak which he read just before he alighted in Grubori and was reading it still then, the statement he made afterwards to the HTV journalist is false?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you are -- first of all, that's -- that is not a question. What you -- apparently the witness did not understand your question. Let me try to rephrase your question. Ms. Mahindaratne sees that there is an inconsistency between what Mr. Cermak said to the journalists compared to what he -- what one finds in your report and whether you have an explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An explanation for this. It is difficult for me to give an explanation for this now, since in the meantime representatives of the special police had arrived, the only explanation is that there existed another report, perhaps theirs, which he read and then mixed up the information he received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you're speculating that, Mr. Dondo. Do you know for a fact that Mr. Cermak had received --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at any stage afterwards did Mr. Cermak tell you that there were -- that your report is wrong or that your findings are incorrect?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: We no longer discussed the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in 2009 when you -- the Defence statement, in paragraph 30 you say, and I have only a few more questions to you about this incident, you say that when the UN civil affairs representative informed you about this incident you told her to report the incident to the civil police and you say, "and I expected her to do that." Now, as a liaison officer, isn't it one of your basic obligations to convey information received from the international -- members of the international organisations to the local authorities, to the Croatian authorities? That's your primary task, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Among others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So why did you pass that obligation on -- back on to the UN monitor who informed you of the incident instead of carrying out your task?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Because he was a member of the civilian structure of the UN and it was my opinion that as such he should have reported to the civilian police. Had he worn a uniform, my view would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you then -- you expected the international community to attend to that and you didn't yourself think it necessary to report the matter to the police? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that we reacted to the information we got from them instantly in several ways, one of them being through General Cermak. However, since the lady was from the civilian service of the UN, I also expected her personally to go to the civilian police as well and give her report in addition to the report we were going to submit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that: "... we reacted to the information we got from them instantly in several ways, one of them being through General Cermak." What did you expect Mr. Cermak to do once you reported the matter to him?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: At any rate, that he would phone the police and ask them if they were aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document P1221, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while that document comes up, Mr. Dondo, I just want to read a portion of your statement given to the OTP in 2005, where you say - and this is in paragraph 31 of D1695 for the record - you say: "It was only later in response to an inquiry from the ICRC that I learned about the suggestion of a fire-fight between terrorists and the special police. I can say that the response from Mr. Cermak to that inquiry seemed to be in a more military tone than was normal for him, but I do not know if he was basing his response on a military or special police briefing or report." Now, this is the document you're referring to in paragraph 25 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 31 of your statement, isn't it, the ICRC inquiry?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I have difficulties in finding it in the English text, what you just read to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I was reading off his statement while the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, his statement, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- D1695, that's the first statement, Mr. President, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the ICRC send this letter to General Cermak via you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes. The ICRC sent a letter via us, asking about the events in Grubori, expecting a response from the general, which ensued in the form in which you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have P1222, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you referred to the response sent by General Cermak to this inquiry, and you say that was the first time you learnt about this alleged fire-fight in Grubori. Now, was it you who conveyed this response of General Cermak to ICRC?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In any event, you say that it was from this letter that you learnt of the fire-fight, and in this letter, if I could -- if you could focus on paragraph 2, it's reported that -- as follows: "During the operation aimed at locating and destroying the defeated enemy sabotage-terrorist groups and locating the MTS, when we were searching the village of Plavno, hamlet of Grubor, we spotted eight to ten enemy soldiers who opened gun-fire at members of the Ministry of the Interior special forces. In the shooting that ensued, Djure Karanovic, aged about 45, a resident of Belgrade was killed; he was carrying a 7.9-millimetre rifle. During the shoot-out the other members of the enemy group fled in the direction of the village of Strmica." Now, you testified here that you didn't see any weapons near any bodies or in Grubori when you conducted your own mission. And according to your report, a person by the name of Djure Karanovic had come for hay-making, you report in your -- according to your own report. Now, when you saw this report -- I'm sorry, Mr. Dondo, are you having trouble about -- having trouble getting reception?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Not anymore. It's okay now. [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you read this report, didn't you ask Mr. Cermak as to from where he got this information? Because clearly what is reported in Mr. Cermak's report to the ICRC is inconsistent with what you had reported to him.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, I did not approach the victims nor did I examine them in such a way as to be able to say that under the bodies or anywhere on their bodies, especially Djure Karanovic which -- whose body was out in the open toward a forest, so we never approached the body itself because it may have been dangerous. We didn't go there to see whether he had a rifle on his body. Secondly, I, as a liaison officer, cannot comment on the general's statements or letters. It is for me to translate it and forward it to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, today when -- please.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I can comment here that in this letter, as I have said before, military terms are used which is not usual, not typical, of General Cermak's style because this is a purely military letter and in his communication, in his letters, he never used that style or that terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you just point us -- point to us what those military terms are which are not used by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes. "Aimed at locating and destroying the defeated enemy sabotage terrorist groups and locating the equipment and materiel when we were searching the village of Plavno ... "In the shooting that ensued, Djure Karanovic, aged about 45 ... was killed. "As a result of the fighting in which a hand-held rocket launcher was used, fire was set to," et cetera ... All these are military terms. This is military language which a businessman and a logistics expert would not use daily in his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, you just -- you've -- in paragraph 31 of your 2005 statement, you say that: "... it is more military tone than was normal for him, but I do not know if he was basing his response on a military or special police briefing or report." So you are merely speculating that, are you not, Mr. Dondo? You do not know what information was the basis for this report that Mr. Cermak sent to ICRC?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Well, certainly I'm speculating. But I am certain that he used -- that he didn't use that terminology usually because I typed many of his letters. I can say that for certain. Whether he received information from the special police or anybody else is a matter of pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you typed his letters, were all his letters dictated by him to you? All the letters sent by General Cermak where you acted as a liaison officer typing and conveying, were they all dictated by Mr. Cermak to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you draft any of his reports or any letters without his authority or without --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you have never drafted any of his letters without his authority, without his instructions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, before we lose ourselves in the further analysis of these kind of matters, perhaps -- the witness has said that this is typically military language. And now to try to analyse the whole of the correspondence of Mr. Cermak, how it was created, how military it was, how non-military it was, and -- might not be of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it is relevant --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It would be relevant, Mr. President, to some other areas which I would discuss later on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I certainly would like to answer the question. Without his permission, nobody in our office or any office of any liaison officer would have drafted a letter of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just on this subject of Grubori, the last question, Mr. Dondo, and I move on. Today, to questions from the Bench - and this is at transcript page 26, line 24 - the Presiding Judge asked you whether what you observed in Grubori was consistent with the content of the report sent by General Cermak to the ICRC. And you answered in the affirmative. You said "yes." I want to take you to your 2005 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if -- Mr. Registrar, if we could have D1695. Before we go to that -- before we -- Mr. Registrar, if you could just keep this document here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I want -- or I'd like you to look at paragraph 3 of this document, Mr. Dondo, it says: "As a result of the fighting in which a hand-held rocket-launcher was used, fire was set to several cattle sheds and houses ..." That's what I wanted to draw your attention to, and then if we could go to your statement -- the testimony, that's D1695. And if we could go to page 11 in the English version, that's paragraph 29. After five lines from the bottom of that paragraph, paragraph 29, you say: "All the bodies were of elderly people and none of them were dressed in military uniform. I also recall the dead animals which I mentioned in my report. I have been asked if I recall any marks on the buildings which might have been caused by bullets, but I cannot recall such marks." So your own observations were in fact not consistent with Mr. Cermak's report to ICRC about a fire-fight in Grubori in the course of which houses were fired at and they caught fire? Isn't that correct, Mr. Dondo? You yourself did not see any evidence on the buildings of a fire-fight?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Here a hand-held -- or hand-held rocket-launchers are mentioned and those set houses on fire. I can confirm that houses were set on fire possibly by the -- by projectiles from rocket-launchers, but I was asked whether I had seen bullet-holes in the walls of the houses and my reply was negative.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't understand your response where you say: "I can confirm that houses were set on fire possibly by projectiles from rocket-launchers." When you say "I can confirm," are you referring to the Grubori incident or are you just merely saying that houses can be -- can catch fire by projectiles? I'm trying to understand what you said there.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that because I'm not a fire-arms expert or an expert for fire-related matters. I can only confirm that houses really had been burnt or had been -- or were burning, but how they were set on fire I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, considering that you didn't see any marks on the buildings that indicated fire-fight -- considering that you did not see any deceased persons in military uniforms or weapons in the area, your own observations, I'm referring to your own observations in Grubori, do not correspond to this version reported by Mr. Cermak. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you answered in the affirmative and the Presiding Judge asked you if your own observations were consistent with this report and you answered in the -- answered "yes," that was incorrect, isn't it? That was wrong?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Your question confuses me. I don't remember the question of the Presiding Judge or, indeed, your question. So if you could repeat I'd be much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you was: When you today, this morning -- the Presiding Judge asked you this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- witness just said that he doesn't remember that question, so before you repeat your question, you perhaps put to him what I asked him and what his answer was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could do it quickly myself as well. Mr. Dondo, I asked you this morning whether the report sent to the Red Cross was consistent with what you had observed personally, and you gave an answer to that question. You said it was consistent. And now, Ms. Mahindaratne, put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So your response to the Presiding Judge that it was consistent is wrong; isn't that correct, Mr. Dondo? In fact, your observations are inconsistent with what Mr. Cermak has reported to ICRC; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I have to think about this because both are practically accurate depending on how you look at it. I repeat, I'm not an expert in fire-arms or in fire-related matters or for the detection of fire-arms. I'm not a criminologist, and therefore I cannot really make conclusions as to who was shooting from where and with what kind of weapons. If you're asking me to give an expert judgement whether rounds were shot from a mortar or any type of fire-arms and whether there were --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, please, I'm not asking you to give any expert conclusions at all. My question is very simple. You saw -- you visited Grubori. You saw bodies. You saw the houses. You conducted your own fact-finding mission. Based on what you found --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- what Mr. Cermak has reported to the ICRC in this report is incorrect; isn't that right? I'm asking you in the context of what you found.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO
utterances.text: I would sooner say that it was correct than incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, your report gives a picture of the situation which is a picture in which hardly, if any, combat context is given, but rather details elderly persons. No reference whatsoever to this being the result of any way of clearing operations or military operations, whereas the report sent to the ICRC puts the whole situation in a clear combat situation. Now, I think that's what Ms. Mahindaratne is interested in to know, whether you consider that the picture given to the ICRC is rather different from the picture you gave, and to that extent inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's inconsistent in that my report was the report of a liaison officer and I was focused on what had happened to people, livestock, and the events that had happened, the people who were killed, rather than an expert analysis what could have produced those consequences or preceded them. And soldiers can say why those things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten about that. Yes, we'll have to adjourn for the day, Mr. Dondo. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is the testimony you've given today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 but in another -- in Courtroom -- the same Courtroom, Courtroom III. Could you perhaps already follow the usher. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you inform the Chamber as to where you stand in terms of time. I think you -- it was earlier indicated that you would need three to four sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe tomorrow morning's session I should be able to finish, Mr. President, just one more session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first session tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can adjourn until -- unless there's any urgent matters to be discussed at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I forgot to make an application to allow the Prosecution to upload the additional translations which we went through the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- that document ID number 06720944 to Exhibit P5226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, should -- upload it to the same document or should we keep them apart and say this is the evidence given at the time by Mr. Cermak and we have additional portions of that meeting translated which are, I take it, then tendered by the Prosecution for the purposes of credibility and reliability of the present witness. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I believe for completion -- in the interests of completeness because the -- P255 -- 2526, the Croatian transcript contains the entire -- all of the exchanges that we want to tender through these additional translations. So it's only the English transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see what it is, but at the time we didn't discuss to have it all in English there because I think we would focus on the statement of Mr. Cermak rather than on any conversations he would have had with others. But I have to go back into the transcript to see whether this was discussed at the time. Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock. If there's anything you'd like to briefly say at this moment, you are invited to do; otherwise, I would ask you to wait until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just on this. We would welcome, so to speak, an upgraded full transcript. I think that would assist all parties in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then to attach this or work it in the English version so that we can read it? What's the best way of proceeding, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe -- I have been informed that the current transcript is in a TIFF form, which means to have it upgraded together, we would have to re-type the entire transcript which would take some time, but that can be done in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then otherwise we would have to jump from one page to another and back again --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and a TIFF, even a TIFF transcript by the technique of OCR can relatively easy -- although it takes some time to check whether the accuracy is sufficient. Could you please explore the possibilities on how much extra work it takes compared to the extra work and the confusion by jumping from one document to another? Because there are many entries which you would have to jump to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, 6th of October, 9.00, Courtroom III, with apologies to any Chamber which is deprived of a couple of minutes this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
